name: Hong Kong
info: Hong Kong is a special administrative region of China on the eastern side of the Pearl River estuary, a farming and fishing area that became a British colony from 1841, then a free port and an industrial and financial centre.

facts.founded: People lived in the area for tens of thousands of years; as a city it grew from the British colony on Hong Kong Island, occupied on 26 January 1841 and formally ceded to the United Kingdom in the Treaty of Nanking in 1842.
facts.where: On China's southern coast, on the eastern side of the Pearl River estuary, 60 km east of Macau and south of Shenzhen, on Hong Kong Island, the Kowloon Peninsula, the New Territories and over 200 other islands.
facts.known: A British colony from 1841 to 1997; a free port and entrepôt; the Japanese occupation of 1941 to 1945; refugees from mainland China; industrialisation in the 1950s; the Sino-British Joint Declaration of 1984; the handover of 1997
facts.today: Hong Kong is a special administrative region of China, with about 7.5 million residents, governed under the principle of one country, two systems.

t: The area was a place of farming and fishing villages under Chinese dynasties until the Qing ceded Hong Kong Island to Britain in 1842 after the First Opium War, and Britain added Kowloon in 1860 and the New Territories on a 99-year lease in 1898.

Refugees from mainland China, especially after 1949, supplied the labour and capital that turned a trading port into an industrial territory in the 1950s and later into a financial and shipping centre.
Under the Sino-British Joint Declaration of 1984 the United Kingdom handed Hong Kong to China at midnight on 1 July 1997, after 156 years of British rule.
dyk: The name first appears in English in 1780 as "He-Ong-Kong" and originally referred to a small inlet near Aberdeen; it is generally believed to render the Cantonese hēung góng, "fragrant harbour" or "incense harbour".
ev: The southern Song court, briefly based near modern Kowloon City, is defeated at the Battle of Yamen by the Yuan
The Treaty of Nanking cedes Hong Kong Island to the United Kingdom in perpetuity
The Convention of Peking gives Britain the Kowloon Peninsula and Stonecutters Island
Britain obtains a 99-year lease of the New Territories
Japan attacks Hong Kong on 8 December and the British surrender on 25 December
The Sino-British Joint Declaration provides for the handover of Hong Kong to China
Hong Kong is handed over to China at midnight on 1 July
The Hong Kong national security law comes into effect on 1 July

sections.origins:
Hong Kong stands on China's southern coast, on the eastern side of the Pearl River estuary, and consists of Hong Kong Island, the Kowloon Peninsula, the New Territories, Lantau Island and over 200 other islands. The earliest known human traces there date to 35,000 to 39,000 years ago, from knapped stone tools found at Wong Tei Tung on the Sai Kung Peninsula in deposits dated by optical luminescence. By the Middle Neolithic period the region had been widely occupied. Early inhabitants are believed to have been Austronesians and later the Yue people, and rice cultivation had been introduced by the Late Neolithic period. Bronze Age settlers made coarse and hard pottery, quartz and stone jewellery and small bronze implements.

The Qin dynasty brought the area into China after conquering the indigenous Baiyue. It was then part of the Nanyue kingdom and was recaptured by China after the Han conquest. In the 13th century the southern Song court was briefly based in modern Kowloon City, where the Sung Wong Toi site stands, before its defeat at the Battle of Yamen in 1279. By the end of the Yuan dynasty seven large families had settled in the region and owned most of the land. The name, first romanised as "He-Ong-Kong" in 1780, originally referred to a small inlet between Aberdeen Island and the south coast of Hong Kong Island, where British sailors first met local fishermen.
sections.growth:
Hong Kong was originally an area of farming and fishing villages. After the British took the island, administrative buildings went up quickly in 1842, but piracy, disease and hostile Qing policies at first kept merchants away. Conditions improved in the 1850s, when the Taiping Rebellion sent many Chinese refugees, including wealthy merchants, to the colony. By the end of the Second Opium War Hong Kong had grown from a transient outpost into a major entrepôt. The Hongkong and Shanghai Bank opened in 1865, the first gas company in 1862 and the first electric company in 1890. The population rose from 530,000 in 1916 to 725,000 in 1925, and the University of Hong Kong was founded in 1911.

After 1949 skilled migrants and capital, especially from Shanghai, and a large pool of cheap labour revived the economy. In the 1950s Hong Kong changed from entrepôt trade to manufacturing, making goods such as buttons, artificial flowers, umbrellas, textiles and plastics. Public housing estates, the Independent Commission Against Corruption, founded in 1974, and the Mass Transit Railway were set up in the post-war decades. As costs rose, manufacturers moved to the mainland, and by the early 1990s Hong Kong had become a financial centre and shipping hub.
sections.rulers:
Under the Qin the area was governed from Panyu County, then it was part of Nanyue and was recaptured by China after the Han conquest. In later centuries it fell under Panyu, Bao'an, Dongguan and finally Xin'an County, until the British arrived. Britain occupied Hong Kong Island on 25 and 26 January 1841 under the Convention of Chuenpi, signed by Charles Elliot and Qishan, which neither government ratified. The Treaty of Nanking of 29 August 1842 ceded the island in perpetuity and it became a crown colony. The Convention of Peking of 1860 added the Kowloon Peninsula and Stonecutters Island, and in 1898 Britain obtained a 99-year lease of the New Territories.

Japan occupied Hong Kong from 23 December 1941 to 15 August 1945, with Isogai Rensuke as its first Japanese governor. The British resumed control in 1945, and the colony kept its form of government through the post-war decades. Governor Murray MacLehose raised the question of Hong Kong's future with Deng Xiaoping in 1979. Chris Patten, appointed in 1992, was the last British governor. The Legislative Council became fully elected for the first time in 1995. At midnight on 1 July 1997, after 156 years of British rule, the United Kingdom handed Hong Kong to the People's Republic of China. Tung Chee Hwa became its first chief executive.
sections.life:
The indigenous inhabitants before 1898 included the Punti, Hakka, Tanka and Hoklo, who had lived in the area for many years. When the British arrived, the population of Hong Kong Island was about 7,450, mostly Tanka fishermen and Hakka charcoal burners in coastal villages. Some clans built walled villages for protection from bandits, rival clans and wild animals. Salt, pearls and fishing had long provided a living. Cantonese later became the predominant language, spoken by 93.7 per cent of the population today, with English the other official language.

Christian missionaries founded many schools and churches. The Hong Kong College of Medicine for Chinese, founded in 1887, graduated Sun Yat-sen in 1892. The third bubonic plague pandemic reached Hong Kong in 1894 and gave a pretext for racial zoning through the Peak Reservation Ordinance. After the Second World War squatter camps spread across the territory for the many migrants. A fire at Shek Kip Mei led Governor Alexander Grantham to a plan for multi-storey public housing, the start of the high-rise building for which the city is known. The Hong Kong Flu of 1968 infected 15 per cent of the population. Cinema and Cantopop grew from the late 1940s and 1970s respectively, and the territory's culture is a hybrid of Eastern and Western traditions.
sections.crises:
The Third Pandemic of bubonic plague struck in 1894. In April 1899 the residents of Kam Tin rebelled against the colonial government and defended the walled village of Kat Hing Wai until British troops blasted open its iron gate. The Japanese attack began on 8 December 1941, eight hours after the attack on Pearl Harbor. British, Canadian and Indian troops and the Hong Kong Volunteer Defence Forces resisted but were outnumbered, and on 25 December, called Black Christmas by locals, Governor Mark Aitchison Young surrendered. During the occupation food was rationed and inflation ran high, and an estimated 10,000 civilians were executed, while many others were tortured, raped or mutilated. The population fell from 1.6 million before the war to 600,000 in 1945.

In the 1967 riots pro-PRC protesters clashed with the colonial government; as many as 51 people were killed and 802 injured, and police and the British military defused as many as 8,000 home-made bombs. After the handover the government used large foreign exchange reserves to hold the currency peg in the Asian financial crisis of 1997, and the territory then had an H5N1 avian-flu outbreak and the 2003 SARS epidemic. A march against the Article 23 security bill drew as many as 750,000 people in 2003 and the bill was shelved. Protests over the electoral system in 2014 became known as the Umbrella Revolution. Protests against an extradition bill began in June 2019, and organisers claimed more than three million took part.
sections.legacy:
Hong Kong was one of the Four Asian Tigers and the first of them to industrialise, in the 1950s. Between 1961 and 1997 its gross domestic product increased by a factor of 180. Its legal system is based on common law, continuing the tradition of British rule, and vehicles still drive on the left. Many buildings of the colonial and earlier periods survive, among them the Tin Hau Temple, first built in 1012 and rebuilt in 1266, the oldest existing structure in the territory, and Flagstaff House of 1846, the oldest Western-style building.

The Sino-British Joint Declaration of 19 December 1984, signed by Margaret Thatcher and Zhao Ziyang, promised that China would keep Hong Kong's economic and political systems for 50 years after the handover under the principle of one country, two systems. The Basic Law, accepted on 4 April 1990, serves as the region's constitution. The national security law came into effect on 1 July 2020, and in March 2021 the National People's Congress changed the electoral system. Hong Kong is today a special administrative region of China of about 7.5 million residents, with its own currency, immigration policy and public finances.

summary: Hong Kong, on China's southern coast, was an area of farming and fishing villages until Britain took the island in 1841 and added Kowloon and the New Territories. Refugees and trade made it an industrial and financial centre. It returned to China in 1997.
references: John Carroll, A Concise History of Hong Kong (Rowman & Littlefield, 2007)
Susanna Hoe, The Taking of Hong Kong: Charles and Clara Elliot in China Waters (Routledge, 1999)
Michael Ingham, Hong Kong: A Cultural History (Oxford University Press, 2007)
Philip Snow, The Fall of Hong Kong: Britain, China and the Japanese Occupation (Yale University Press, 2003)
Steve Tsang, A Modern History of Hong Kong (I.B. Tauris, 2007)
notes: START: 1841 chosen as the British occupation of Hong Kong Island (26 January 1841 in the main article; the History article says 25 January). The Treaty of Nanking (1842) is the formal cession. The area was inhabited long before; the earliest traces are given as 35,000-39,000 years ago (main) and over 30,000 years (History); I used the main article's range only in the origins section.

DISAGREEMENT left out: the Qin incorporation is dated 214 BCE in the main article and 'loosely' under the Qin dynasty (221-206 BCE) in the History article; I gave no year. Neolithic settlement is 'about 6,000 years ago' (main) vs 'approximately 7,000 years ago' (History); no figure given. The History article names the Che people as Neolithic settlers; the main article says Austronesians then Yue: I used the main article's wording.

DISAGREEMENT: British resumption of control on 30 August 1945 (main) vs liberation by joint British and Chinese troops, with the occupation ending 15 August 1945 (History). I gave 15 August as the end of occupation (History) and 'resumed control in 1945' without a day.

DISAGREEMENT: the occupation of the island is 25 January 1841 (History) vs 26 January 1841 (main, and the Union Jack raised 26 January 1841 in History's imperial section). I wrote '25 and 26 January 1841'.

The History article's Hong Kong Island population of about 7,450 refers to 1841. The 8,000 bombs figure (one in eight genuine) is from History; the 51 killed and 802 injured of 1967 from the main article, which says dozens were killed by police: not repeated.

Events since 1997 are given as bare dated facts as the articles state them: Article 23 march (History: 'as many as 750,000 people', 1 July 2003; the main article says the bill was unsuccessfully attempted), 2014 protests, the 2019 extradition bill protests (organisers' claim of more than three million, attributed), the national security law of 1 July 2020, the electoral changes of March 2021. Left out for neutrality: the Apple Daily closure, arrests, the National Anthem Ordinance, the 2023 District Council reforms, the 2024 ordinance, and the articles' evaluations of these laws.
The 'today' sentence uses the lead's 7.5 million; the demographics section gives 7,413,070 in 2021. No 'as of' year written.
'The first bubonic plague pandemic of 1894 ... pretext for racial zoning' is the History article's phrasing ('provided the pretext for racial zoning'); written as given.
Tin Hau Temple 'originally built in 1012 and rebuilt in 1266' from the main article. Cantopop and cinema dates from the main article (cinema hub from the late 1940s; Cantopop emerged in the 1970s).

Left out: tourism, rankings, skyscraper records, airport, sport, financial-centre standings, COVID-19, billionaire and income figures. The main article's 'GDP increased by a factor of 180' (1961 to 1997) kept as a lasting economic fact.

Hong Kong was a crown colony 'in perpetuity' for the island only; Kowloon (1860) is described as ceded in History's lead but as a 'perpetual lease' in its section on the lease; I wrote 'added' for Kowloon.
The 'rulers' sentence on county governance (Panyu, Bao'an, Dongguan, Xin'an) is from the History article; the dates are not given beyond the dynasties and are omitted.
